def: Copying facts out of a document into the boxes of a table, so nobody has to retype them.
here: Each work order has 9 boxes: work order number, date, equipment, serial number, what broke, labor hours, parts cost, priority and warranty claim.

def: One box to fill in, such as "Parts cost".
here: 9 boxes x 50 documents = 450 boxes scored.

def: The correct answers, written down at the moment the practice documents were made.
here: The AI and the plain rules never saw it. It is only used afterwards, to mark their work.

def: Of the answers it gave, the share that were right. High precision means few wrong answers.
here: On new forms the AI gave 217 answers and 204 were right: 94.0%.

def: Of the facts really in the documents, the share it found and got right. High recall means little is missed.
here: On new forms there were 222 facts; the AI found 204 (91.9%) and the plain rules 91 (41.0%).

term: Familiar vs new forms (seen vs unseen)
def: Familiar forms use the layouts the plain rules were written against. New forms use different labels, wording and date styles that neither method was tuned on.
here: Documents 1 to 25 are familiar; 26 to 50 are new. The new half is the fair test of "what happens when next month's forms look different".

def: The shape of a document: a labelled form, a short table, or a free-text email or note.
here: 3 layouts, each in a familiar and a new style.

def: Hand-written search patterns, such as "take the text after Serial No.". Fast and predictable, but they break when the wording changes.
here: The baseline the AI has to beat, and its safety net when the AI fails.

def: A compact way to write a text search pattern, used to build the plain rules.
here: See extractor/rules.py.

def: A program trained on a great deal of text that can read a document and answer in words. ChatGPT is a famous, very large one that runs in the cloud.
here: This project uses Gemma 3 with 4 billion parameters (gemma3:4b, about 3.3 GB), small enough to run on a laptop's ordinary processor.

def: An AI model that runs on your own computer instead of a company's servers. Your documents do not have to travel anywhere to be read.
here: The model runs in Ollama on the same PC.

def: A computer's name for itself (also written 127.0.0.1). A program that only talks to localhost is talking to another program on the same machine.
here: The extractor refuses to send text to any address other than localhost, 127.0.0.1 or ::1, and a test checks that.

def: A free program that downloads AI models once and then runs them on your own computer.
here: It needs the internet once, to download the model. Reading documents does not.

def: Turning a picture of text, such as a scan or a fax, into real text a computer can read.
here: This project does NOT do OCR yet. It reads PDFs that already contain text. Real scans would need an OCR step first.

def: When an AI confidently states something that is not in its source.
here: 3 invented dates in 450 boxes; 0 invented or wrong numbers in the 100 hours and cost boxes.

def: Checks on every answer before it is kept: a real date, a known category, a sensible number.
here: If an answer fails, the AI is shown the error and tries again, up to 3 times (pydantic does the checking).

def: A backup plan that takes over when the main method fails.
here: After 3 failed AI answers the plain rules answer instead, so one bad document never stops the batch. It happened once (doc_043).

def: Realistic but invented data, made by a program so that no real person, client or company is involved.
here: All 50 work orders are SYNTHETIC, made by a seeded generator.

def: Records a government publishes for anyone to use.
here: FDA recall notices and NHTSA vehicle recalls. They test the AI on real-world text.

def: US Food and Drug Administration. It publishes food and drug recall notices.
here: 10 recall reasons scraped from one FDA page and sorted into categories by the AI.

def: US National Highway Traffic Safety Administration. It publishes vehicle safety recalls.
here: 35 recalls; NHTSA's own label for the broken part is the answer key. The AI matched 31.

def: A document describing how an office protects client information: who can see it, where it is stored, how it is backed up and thrown away.
here: Tax preparers must keep one under the FTC Safeguards Rule. IRS Publication 5708 is a free template.

def: A US rule (16 CFR Part 314) requiring financial businesses, including tax preparers of any size, to protect customer information and keep a written security plan.
here: This site does not claim the tool makes anyone compliant. It can help an office describe the tool in its own plan.

def: American Bar Association guidance (July 2024) on lawyers using generative AI, including getting a client's informed consent before putting their information into a self-learning AI tool.
here: Whether a local, non-learning model needs that consent is a legal question for the firm, not something this site answers.

def: DuckDB is a small database that lives in one file on your computer. A CSV file is a plain table that Excel and Power BI open.
here: The finished tables are written to both, on the same PC.
